name: High vs low self-esteem diagnosis via emotional diversification and sabotage patterns
definition: Self-esteem (more accurately: deservingness) determines how someone handles emotional closeness. High self-esteem people seek closeness, want one partner to fulfill all needs, and display self-respect/transparency/strong boundaries. Low self-esteem people believe they're not inherently likable (people like them for extrinsic things: looks, money, skills), so they diversify emotional needs across multiple partners to feel safer, sabotage perfect situations hoping to be pursued, and form transactional relationships. Detection: check for emotional diversification (men: rotation; women: orbiters—one guy for friendship, one for money, one for sex). Self-esteem may be domain-specific and possibly an offshoot of competence—speaker has HSE in dating (knows he's irreplaceable) but LSE in business (hedges, stutters, afraid to set boundaries).
core_claim: If someone diversifies emotional needs across multiple partners instead of consolidating them, then they have low self-esteem, because they don't believe they deserve to have all needs met by one person and fear losing everything if that one person leaves. This manifests as men keeping rotations, women keeping orbiters (best friend guy + provider guy + sex guy), and sabotaging perfect situations hoping to be pursued.

idea_origin.event_summary: Speaker describes this as the single principle that changed his life most. Used to be low self-esteem: wanted validation, chased hottest girls even if bad for him, only dated women with boyfriends/husbands to avoid responsibility for all their needs. Now has high self-esteem in dating but notices it doesn't carry over to business.
idea_origin.trigger: Noticing the contrast between how he handles dating (self-respect, transparency, strong boundaries, knows he's irreplaceable) vs business (hedges, stutters in meetings, scared to set boundaries with boss, indirect communication).
idea_origin.lesson_learned: Self-esteem is domain-specific. Speaker got really good at dating before developing self-esteem there. The question remains: is self-esteem an offshoot of competence? High self-esteem appears after proving you're skilled, unique, and irreplaceable in that domain.

canonical_instruction: Identify if the user is exhibiting HSE or LSE patterns by checking: (1) Do they consolidate emotional/professional needs in one source or diversify across many? (2) Do they sabotage good situations hoping to be pursued? (3) Are their relationships transactional or connection-based? (4) Do they believe people like them for them or for extrinsic value? Map their behavior to the HSE pattern (seeks closeness, consolidates, transparent boundaries) or LSE pattern (diversifies, sabotages, transactional, believes they're liked for extrinsic things). If LSE, note that building competence in the domain may precede self-esteem development.

audiences: people who keep rotations or orbiters
people confident in one domain but not another
situations: diagnosing why someone keeps sabotaging good things
understanding why confidence doesn't transfer across domains
exclusions: clinical attachment disorders requiring professional treatment
situations where diversification is genuinely strategic not fear-based

transformation_rules: List the user's current emotional/professional need sources and check if consolidated or diversified
Check for sabotage pattern: do they push away or test good situations?
Check relationship basis: connection-based (HSE) or transactional/extrinsic (LSE)?
Classify as HSE or LSE based on these patterns
If LSE, identify if they've built competence in the domain yet
Note that self-esteem may develop after competence is established
tests: Output identifies emotional diversification pattern (rotation for men, orbiters for women)
Output mentions the specific orbiter roles if applicable (best friend guy, provider guy, sex guy)
Output distinguishes transactional relationships from connection-based ones
Output acknowledges domain-specificity of self-esteem (can be HSE in dating, LSE in business)
No generic self-esteem advice without mapping to specific HSE/LSE behavioral indicators
counterexamples: Strategic diversification that isn't fear-based (e.g., networking intentionally)
Genuine polyamory based on preference not fear of consolidation
Clinical attachment disorders beyond this framework's scope
input_triggers: keeping a rotation of partners instead of committing
having multiple orbiters who each serve different functions
believing people only like you for your skills/looks/money not for you
only going for unavailable people (with boyfriends, married)
confident in dating but stutter in business meetings
scared to set boundaries with boss but not with romantic partners

related.note: Self-esteem being domain-specific connects to stable vs dynamic domains—HSE in dating (stable) doesn't transfer to business (dynamic)

components.name: HSE seeks emotional consolidation; LSE diversifies across partners
components.applies_when: Diagnosing whether someone is HSE or LSE based on how they distribute emotional needs

components.name: LSE sabotages perfect situations hoping to be pursued
components.applies_when: Someone pushes away good partners/opportunities and creates drama to test if they'll be chased

components.name: LSE believes likability is extrinsic (looks/money/skills) not intrinsic
components.applies_when: Someone believes partners only want them for what they provide, not who they are

components.name: HSE displays self-respect, transparency, and strong boundaries
components.applies_when: Someone tells people immediately when they did something wrong, is direct in communication

components.name: Self-esteem may be an offshoot of proven competence in that domain
components.applies_when: Speaker developed HSE in dating only after getting really good at it first; suggests competence precedes self-esteem

components.name: Emotional diversification pattern: orbiters (woman) or rotation (man)
components.applies_when: Woman has: one guy = best friend, one guy = pays for stuff, one guy = sex. Man keeps girls in rotation, fears commitment.
